slides.title: What is a lemonade stand?
slides.text: A lemonade stand is a tiny business — you make something (lemonade!) and sell it to people who want to buy it. For example, on a hot day you might set up a little table outside with a pitcher of lemonade and a sign, and neighbors walking by can stop and buy a cup.

slides.title: What is trading?
slides.text: Trading means giving someone something they want, and getting something you want back — like a coin for a cup of lemonade. For example, your neighbor gives you a coin, and you give them a cold cup of lemonade in return — both of you end up happy with the trade.

slides.title: Where ideas come from
slides.text: A business often starts with a simple idea — like noticing people get thirsty and thinking, 'I could sell them a cold drink!' For example, if you notice people walking their dogs past your house every morning looking tired and hot, that's exactly the kind of noticing that could turn into a lemonade stand idea.

slides.title: Who is a customer?
slides.text: A customer is someone who buys what you're selling. Being friendly and helpful makes customers want to come back. For example, if you smile and say "thank you, have a great day!" to everyone who buys lemonade, they're much more likely to stop by your stand again next time.

slides.title: You can make things too!
slides.text: Drawing pictures, making bracelets, or baking cookies to share or sell are all little ways of being an entrepreneur — someone who makes and offers things. For example, if you make friendship bracelets and a few classmates want to trade a small toy or a coin for one, you're already being a little entrepreneur.

slides.title: It takes effort
slides.text: Making a lemonade stand work takes real effort — squeezing lemons, making a sign, and standing there smiling at customers! For example, before you sell a single cup, you might spend 20 minutes squeezing lemons, another 10 minutes making a colorful sign, and then stand outside for an hour waiting for customers to come by.

slides.title: Making something to sell
slides.text: Before you can sell something, you have to make it first — like squeezing the lemons and mixing in sugar and water to actually make the lemonade. For example, you can't sell a single cup of lemonade until you've actually squeezed the lemons, added sugar and water, and stirred it all together first.

slides.title: A happy customer comes back
slides.text: When a customer really likes what you sold them, they often want to come back and buy from you again. For example, if your neighbor loves your lemonade so much that they tell you "that was the best lemonade I've ever had," chances are they'll stop by again the next time you open your stand.

slides.title: Spotting a problem to solve
slides.text: Good business ideas often start by spotting a problem — like 'nobody sells cold water at the park' — and figuring out how to fix it. For example, if you notice that kids playing soccer at the park have nowhere nearby to buy a cold drink on a hot day, that gap is exactly the kind of problem a small business could solve.

slides.title: Cost vs. price
slides.text: Cost is what it takes to make something (like lemons and sugar). Price is what you charge someone to buy it. The difference is your profit. For example, if a cup of lemonade costs you 20 cents to make (lemons, sugar, and a cup) and you sell it for $1, your profit on that one cup is 80 cents.

slides.title: A simple plan
slides.text: Before starting, it helps to plan: what will you sell, how much will it cost to make, and how much will you charge? For example, a simple plan might say: "I'll sell lemonade, it costs 20 cents a cup to make, and I'll charge $1 a cup" — writing that down before you start avoids confusion later.

slides.title: Good customer service
slides.text: Being friendly, honest, and helpful makes people want to buy from you again — and tell their friends about you too. For example, if a customer asks for less sugar in their lemonade and you happily make it exactly how they like it, they're likely to become a repeat customer and mention your stand to others.

slides.title: Telling people about it
slides.text: Even a great product needs people to know it exists! A colorful sign or telling your neighbors is a simple form of marketing. For example, making a bright poster that says "Cold Lemonade — $1!" and putting it where people walking by can see it is a simple way to let people know your stand exists.

slides.title: Keeping track
slides.text: Writing down what you spent and what you earned helps you see if your little business is actually making money. For example, if you write down "spent $4 on lemons and sugar, earned $12 selling cups," you can quickly see you made an $8 profit for the day.

slides.title: Trying again if it doesn't work
slides.text: If a business idea doesn't work the first time, entrepreneurs often tweak it and try again instead of giving up. For example, if nobody stopped at your lemonade stand on a cloudy day, you might try moving to a sunnier spot or adding a fun new flavor next time instead of giving up on the idea completely.

slides.title: Making your product special
slides.text: Adding something unique — like a fun flavor of lemonade nobody else has — can make customers pick your stand over anyone else's. For example, adding a splash of strawberry or mint to your lemonade, something the other kids' stands down the street don't offer, could be exactly why customers choose your stand.

slides.title: Planning your day
slides.text: Deciding when to open your stand, how much lemonade to make, and what supplies you need ahead of time helps the whole day run more smoothly. For example, deciding the night before to open from 2-4pm, make one full pitcher, and bring 20 cups means you won't be scrambling to figure things out once customers start showing up.

slides.title: Profit and loss
slides.text: If you earn more than you spend, that's a profit. If you spend more than you earn, that's a loss. Tracking both helps a business survive. For example, if your dog-walking side business earns $60 in a month but spent $75 on flyers, leashes, and treats, that month was actually a $15 loss, even though $60 sounds like good money.

slides.title: Knowing your customer
slides.text: Successful businesses understand who they're selling to — what that person likes, needs, and is willing to pay for. For example, if you're selling handmade bookmarks, knowing that your customers are mostly classmates who love a specific book series could help you design bookmarks featuring those characters, which they'd be far more excited to buy.

slides.title: Teamwork in business
slides.text: Many businesses run better with a team — different people handling different jobs, like making the product, selling it, and managing money. For example, if you and a friend start a dog-walking business together, one of you could focus on finding new customers while the other tracks the schedule and money — splitting the work makes it easier to grow.

slides.title: Taking a smart risk
slides.text: Starting a business always involves some risk — it might not work. Smart entrepreneurs take risks they can afford, not risks that could ruin them. For example, spending $10 of your own savings to try selling friendship bracelets at a school fair is a smart, affordable risk — spending your entire year's savings on the same idea would not be.

slides.title: Reinvesting in growth
slides.text: Instead of spending all the profit right away, many entrepreneurs put some of it back into the business — better supplies, a nicer sign, more inventory. For example, if your bracelet business earns $20 profit one week, using $10 of it to buy more beads and string for next week (instead of spending it all on yourself) helps the business keep growing.

slides.title: Standing out from competitors
slides.text: If other people sell something similar, a business needs a reason customers should pick them — better quality, price, or service. For example, if three kids at your school are all selling friendship bracelets, offering custom colors made to order, or slightly better prices, gives customers a specific reason to choose you.

slides.title: Word of mouth
slides.text: Happy customers telling their friends is one of the most powerful (and free!) ways a small business grows. For example, if one classmate loves the bracelet you made them and shows five friends at lunch, you might suddenly have five new customers without spending a single cent on advertising.

slides.title: Building a name people remember
slides.text: A consistent name, look, or feel for your business — sometimes called a brand — helps customers recognize and trust you again next time. For example, always using the same logo sticker and the same colorful packaging for your bracelets helps customers instantly recognize "oh, that's from her bracelet business" when they see it.

slides.title: Selling online with help
slides.text: With a parent's help, some young entrepreneurs sell crafts or art through simple online marketplaces, reaching far more people than a stand on the street. For example, a 12-year-old who makes custom drawings might, with a parent's account and supervision, list a few pieces online and reach buyers far beyond just their own neighborhood.

slides.title: What is a business plan?
slides.text: A business plan lays out what a business will sell, who it's for, how it'll make money, and what it needs to get started — a roadmap for turning an idea into reality. For example, a teen wanting to start a pet-sitting business might write a one-page plan covering who their customers are (nearby pet owners), how much they'll charge per visit, and what supplies (a leash, treats, a scheduling app) they need first.

slides.title: Startup vs. small business
slides.text: A small business often grows steadily and stays similar in size. A startup usually aims to grow very fast, often testing a new idea that hasn't been proven yet. For example, a local pet-sitting business run by one teen is a small business, growing steadily one customer at a time — while an app trying to connect thousands of pet owners with sitters nationwide, aiming to grow fast, would be more like a startup.

slides.title: Where funding comes from
slides.text: Businesses can be funded with personal savings, loans, or investors who give money in exchange for a share of future profits or ownership. For example, a teen might use $50 of their own savings to buy initial supplies, while a bigger startup might convince an investor to provide $50,000 in exchange for owning 10% of the company.

slides.title: What does "scaling" mean?
slides.text: Scaling means growing a business to serve many more customers without everything becoming proportionally more expensive or difficult to manage. For example, a tutoring business that only earns more by adding more of the tutor's own hours doesn't scale well, but selling a recorded video course that hundreds of students can buy without extra work per student scales much better.

slides.title: Failure is part of the process
slides.text: Many successful entrepreneurs failed at a first (or second, or third) attempt. Learning from what went wrong is often what makes the next attempt succeed. For example, a teen's first attempt at selling custom phone cases online might flop due to poor photos and unclear pricing — but applying those exact lessons to a second attempt often leads to real success.

slides.title: Ethics in business
slides.text: Long-term success usually depends on being honest with customers, treating employees fairly, and not cutting corners just to make a quick profit. For example, honestly describing a product's condition, even when a vague description might sell it faster, builds the kind of trust that keeps customers coming back for years.

slides.title: Solving a real problem
slides.text: The most durable businesses tend to solve a genuine problem for people — not just chase a trend that might fade quickly. For example, a tutoring business solving a real, ongoing need (students struggling with math) tends to last far longer than a business built around a fad that's popular for a few months and then forgotten.

slides.title: Resilience and persistence
slides.text: Markets change, plans fail, and competitors appear. Entrepreneurs who adapt and keep going tend to outlast those who give up at the first setback. For example, if a new competitor undercuts your prices, adapting by improving your service or finding a new customer niche is more likely to succeed than simply giving up.

slides.title: Businesses that also help others
slides.text: Some entrepreneurs build 'social enterprises' — businesses designed to make money while also solving a social or environmental problem, not purely for profit. For example, a teen-run business that sells reusable water bottles and donates a portion of every sale to a clean-water charity is pursuing both profit and positive impact at the same time.

slides.title: Measuring success beyond money
slides.text: Revenue matters, but many entrepreneurs also track customer satisfaction, repeat business, and real-world impact as signs their business is genuinely succeeding. For example, a business that earns a modest profit but has 90% of customers coming back again and again is arguably in a stronger position than one earning more but constantly losing and replacing one-time customers.
